At 3:17 every morning, the moon lowered itself into the harbor.

No one knew why. The fishermen said it was checking the tides. The children said it was thirsty. Old Mara, who had lived in the blue house at the end of Pier Nine for seventy-two years, said the moon was lonely and came down to see if anyone was awake.

She was.

Every night, Mara carried a chair to the end of the pier and waited. She brought a thermos of tea, two biscuits wrapped in wax paper, and a small brass bell she had found in a drawer after her husband died. The bell had no clapper, but sometimes, when the moon touched the water, it rang anyway.

The first time the moon descended, Mara had been twenty-six. She had been standing on the shore with a suitcase in one hand and a train ticket in the other, deciding whether to leave the town forever. The moonlight spilled across the harbor like a road. She stepped onto it.

For a moment, she was somewhere else: a city of glass towers, a room with tall windows, a garden full of oranges. She saw a life that might have been hers. In that life, she was married to someone who laughed easily. She had two daughters. She wrote books. She traveled by train through countries whose names she could not pronounce.

Then the moon rose back into the sky, and Mara was standing on the wet stones with her suitcase at her feet.

She stayed.

Not because the other life was less beautiful, but because this one was real in a way the other could never be. In this life, there was a cracked teacup with her initials on it. There was a neighbor who needed help lifting coal. There was a boy who would someday become her husband, though he had not yet learned how to look at her without blushing.

Years passed. The town changed its name, then changed it back. The cannery closed. The lighthouse became a hotel. People began carrying tiny glowing rectangles in their pockets and stopped looking at the stars.

But the moon kept coming down.

Tonight, Mara is ninety-eight. Her hands tremble as she pours the tea. The harbor is dark except for the moon’s reflection, brightening, widening, becoming solid beneath the pier.

She hears footsteps behind her.

A young man stands at the entrance to the dock, holding a suitcase.

Mara smiles.

“Deciding whether to leave?” she asks.

He looks startled. “How did you know?”

“Everyone comes here for the same reason.”

The moon touches the water.

The brass bell rings.

And somewhere beneath the surface, an entire possible life opens its eyes.
